children: The American Bar Association's status as the federally recognized accreditor of US law schools remained in limbo on Wednesday after a US Department of Education committee failed to reach consensus on ending or renewing its role following seven hours of discussion and debate in Washington.

The 18-member committee opted to revisit the matter on Thursday after holding two deadlocked votes on whether or not to strip law school oversight functions from the attorney organization, which has been enmeshed in a series of clashes with President Donald Trump's administration.

The ABA's legal education council appeared at Wednesday's hearing before the Education Department's bipartisan National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity and argued its status should be renewed. Several committee members said the accreditor was too intertwined with its parent trade organization, however, citing the ability of the larger ABA's policymaking body to weigh in on accreditation standards.

Daniel Thies, the past chair of the legal education council, repeatedly countered that the council was in compliance with Education Department rules and that it has taken additional steps in recent months to become more independent.

The ABA is the country's most-recognized attorney organization, with about 150,000 dues-paying members. Its legal education council, which became the government's recognized accreditor of law schools in 1952 and currently accredits 198 US schools, largely operates separately from the wider ABA. But it has drawn Trump administration criticism amid a federal crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion policies in government, the private sector and academia.

Trump signed an executive order in April 2025 directing Education Secretary ⁠Linda McMahon to assess whether to suspend or terminate the ABA as the government’s official law school accreditor, citing its “unlawful" DEI requirements. Under rules the ABA repealed earlier this month, ABA-accredited schools were required to demonstrate their commitment to diversity in recruitment, admissions and student programming.

Trump and the ABA have separately clashed over his executive orders targeting law firms and his officials’ statements criticizing judges. The ⁠US Department of Justice has barred its attorneys from speaking at or attending ABA events and curtailed the ABA’s longtime role in vetting judicial nominees. A White House spokesperson in 2025 dismissed the organization as a “snooty” group of “leftist lawyers.”

Even if the committee makes a recommendation Thursday, a final decision on the ABA legal education council's accreditor status is not expected for several months. The department reviews higher education accreditors every five years.
AGENCY SAYS ACCREDITATION ARM NOT INDEPENDENT

In an August report recommending against renewing the ABA’s accreditor status, Education Department staff concluded that the legal education council is not "separate and independent" from the larger ABA as required. The report also faulted the ABA for being too slow to revise its law school diversity rule.
Melissa Hart, chair of the ABA’s legal education council, said in a statement that it has “consistently complied” with the Education Department’s requirements.
The Education Department did not respond to a request for comment ahead of Wednesday's meeting.

Revoking the ABA's accreditor status would disrupt federal student loan access for some law schools and could make it harder for law students to take the bar exam and become licensed attorneys in different states.
